sources.title: Mikhail Lyubich, Conformal Geometry and Dynamics of Quadratic Polynomials, vol. I (book draft, Stony Brook)
sources.locator: Ch. 2 §14.1-§14.6, printed pp. 195-198 (PDF pp. 194-197), §14.10.1-§14.10.3, printed pp. 200-201 (PDF pp. 199-200) and the weak-topology background of §13.7.2, printed p. 195 (PDF p. 194); all named results in this range were read in the source.

contents.name: Measurable Riemann Mapping Theorem, printed p. 195: every measurable Beltrami differential with $\|\mu\|_\infty<1$ on $\widehat{\mathbb C}$ has a quasiconformal solution, unique up to postcomposition with a Moebius automorphism and unique after fixing three points
Theorem 14.1 (semi-local integrability), printed p. 195: a measurable coefficient on a domain has a quasiconformal solution unique up to postcomposition with a conformal map
§14.1 Uniqueness, printed p. 196: two solutions differing by a conformal map because their quotient satisfies $\bar\partial=0$, so Weyl's lemma applies

§14.2 Local vs global, printed p. 196: local solutions glue to a complex analytic atlas on the sphere whose transition maps are conformal, and all complex analytic structures on $S^2$ are equivalent by the uniformization theorem

§14.3 Strategy, printed p. 196: solve first for smooth/real-analytic coefficients by local solutions and uniformization, then approximate a measurable coefficient and use compactness of normalized quasiconformal maps

§14.4 Real analytic case, printed pp. 196-197: the complexified equation is solved by characteristics and a nonsingular first integral; the local solution is a nondegenerate real-analytic diffeomorphism

§14.5 Approximation, printed pp. 197-198: approximating coefficients with uniformly bounded dilatation, precompactness of normalized solutions, and the weak-limit argument $\mu_n\partial h_n\rightharpoonup\mu\varphi$ identifying the limit's Beltrami differential

§14.6 Conformal and complex structures, printed p. 198: measurable Beltrami differentials as the data of a conformal structure, with chart expressions of bounded dilatation on a quasiconformal surface
§14.7 Explicit formula (Theorem 14.4), printed pp. 198-199: $h=\mathrm{id}+T(I-\mu S)^{-1}(\mu)$ with the Hilbert transform $S$ unitary on $L^2$
contents.reason: This is the Beurling-transform route the binding design declines for this page: it requires the $L^p$ bounds of the Hilbert transform and invertibility of $I-\mu S$ on $L^2$, neither of which is proved here; the local Holder contraction and the approximation route are used instead.

contents.name: §14.8 Dependence on parameters (Proposition 14.5, Theorem 14.6, Corollaries 14.7-14.8), printed pp. 199-200: continuity and holomorphic dependence of normalized solutions on the coefficient
contents.reason: Holomorphic dependence of Beltrami solutions is Teichmuller/deformation theory, which the design places after this pair (Lyubich §§14.7-14.9) and which no item on this page uses.

contents.name: §14.9 Quasiregular maps, printed p. 200: quasiregular maps factor as a quasiconformal map followed by a holomorphic map
contents.reason: The general quasiregular factorization theory is not needed by any claim on this page; the holomorphy of the weak-solution factor is proved directly by Weyl's lemma in the factorization lemma, and the general quasiregular theory has no page in this run's frontier.

contents.name:
§14.10.1 Solution of the $ ar\partial$-equation (Theorem 14.11), printed pp. 200-201: the Cauchy transform $T
u(z)=- rac1\pi\int
u(\zeta)/(\zeta-z)\,dm(\zeta)$ solves $ ar\partial v=
u$ with the normalisation $c/z$ at infinity
§14.10.2 Fourier transform, printed p. 201: definition and unitarity of the Fourier transform and its conjugation of $\partial$ and $\bar\partial$ to multiplication operators
contents.reason: The Fourier calculus is used in the source only to construct the Hilbert transform as an $L^2$ isometry; the page needs no $L^2$ boundedness of a singular integral and proves its fixed-support Holder bound directly from the Newtonian potential.

contents.name: §14.10.3 Hilbert transform, printed p. 201: the principal-value operator $S\varphi(z)=-\frac1\pi\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\int_{|\zeta-z|>\varepsilon}\varphi(\zeta)/(\zeta-z)^2\,dm$ and its unitary extension
contents.reason: The $L^2$ isometry of the Hilbert/Beurling transform is the operator-theoretic input of the declined Beurling route; this page's Cauchy-transform lemma asserts only the fixed-support Holder bound and its principal-value representation, with no $L^p$ mapping claim.

contents.name: §13.7.2 Weak topologies, printed p. 195: weak and weak-star convergence, weak-star compactness of the dual unit ball and weak-sequential compactness used in the approximation step
Chapter 2 section 14.6, printed page 198: measurable Beltrami differentials give conformal-structure data with chart expressions; used here to relate inversion to the sphere-chart convention.

sources.title: Christopher J. Bishop, Quasiconformal Mappings (Stony Brook Math 627 course notes, 164 pp.)
sources.locator: Ch. 2 §1-§2, printed pp. 47-55, and Ch. 3 §1-§6, printed pp. 85-105 (PDF pp. 55-60 and 89-110); all named results in this range were read in the source.

contents.name: Ch. 2 §1, printed pp. 50-51: the composition rule $\mu_{g\circ f}=(f_z/\bar f_z)(\mu_g-\mu_f)/(1-\mu_g\bar\mu_f)$ and the transformation of the complex dilatation under a change of coordinates
Ch. 2 §2, printed pp. 51-55: the geometric definition of quasiconformality, the piecewise differentiable criterion and Corollary 2.2 on annuli
contents.reason: The geometric definition, its piecewise-differentiable criterion and the annulus corollary are the subject of the preceding extremal-length pair (batch 12) of this run, scaffolded and authored there; no item on this page uses them directly.

contents.name: Ch. 3 §1 Piecewise affine maps, printed p. 85: the unique affine map between two similarly labelled triangles and its dilatation $K=(1+|\mu|)/(1-|\mu|)$, $\mu=\beta/\alpha$

Ch. 3 §2 The mapping theorem, printed pp. 85-88: Theorem 2.1 (continuous coefficients), Corollaries 2.5-2.7, Propositions 2.9-2.10 and Theorem 2.11 (the measurable case by approximation and normalized compactness)
Ch. 3 §3 Covering lemmas and maximal theorems, printed pp. 89-90: Wiener's and Vitali's covering lemmas, Calderon-Zygmund decomposition, the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function

Ch. 3 §4, printed pp. 95–96: Lemma 4.4 (the square Jacobian-area lower bound) and Corollary 4.5 (the resulting f_z L² bound); the a.e. differentiability interface is held open under the current batch-12 source review.
Ch. 3 §5 Gehring's inequality and Bojarski's theorem, printed pp. 97-104: the reverse Holder self-improvement and the $L^p$ (p>2) regularity of the derivatives of a quasiconformal map
contents.reason: This is the $L^p$-self-improvement route to regularity, together with the Hardy-Littlewood and Calderon-Zygmund machinery behind it; the page proves its regularity result from the fixed-support Holder contraction instead and asserts no $p>2$ claim.

contents.name: Ch. 3 §6 Convergence of maps implies convergence of dilatations, printed pp. 103-105: Theorem 6.1, uniform convergence plus a.e. convergence of dilatations gives $\mu_f=\mu$ a.e.
Ch. 2 section 1, printed pages 50–51: conformal precomposition rotates the coefficient phase by twice the negative input angle, and the half-phase gives the ellipse major-axis line.

sources.title: Kari Astala, Albert Clop, Daniel Faraco, Jarmo Jaaskelainen and Aleksis Koski, Nonlinear Beltrami operators, Schauder estimates and bounds for the Jacobian, Ann. Inst. H. Poincare Anal. Non Lineaire 34 (2017), 1543-1559
sources.locator: Introduction and Theorems 1.1-1.3, printed pp. 1543-1545; §2.1-§2.4, printed pp. 1545-1554; §3, printed pp. 1554-1556 (all read in the source).

contents.name: Introduction, printed p. 1544: in the linear case $H(z,\xi)=\mu(z)\xi$ the assumption (1.2) implies $\alpha$-Holder continuity of the derivatives and a nonvanishing Jacobian for homeomorphic solutions
Theorem 1.1, printed p. 1544: a homeomorphic solution has positive Jacobian, with a lower bound on $D(0,R_0)$ for a normalized solution
Theorem 1.2, printed p. 1545: Schauder estimates for the nonlinear equation with $\gamma=\alpha$ if $\alpha<1/K$ and any $\gamma<1/K$ otherwise
contents.reason: The theorem is nonlinear, and its explicit ellipticity-limited exponent $\gamma<1/K$ is exactly what the owner direction forbids replacing the linear exponent $\alpha$ by; the page keeps the full linear exponent proved by the fixed-support Holder contraction.

contents.name: Theorem 1.3, printed p. 1545: if $\xi\mapsto H(z,\xi)$ is $C^1$, the exponent restriction disappears and solutions are $C^{1,\alpha}_{\mathrm{loc}}$
contents.reason: The proof of Theorem 1.3 requires the extra nonlinear Morrey-Campanato machinery of §2.4; the linear case, which is what this page promises, is proved here constructively from the published Newtonian-potential estimate and needs none of it.

contents.name: Propositions 2.1-2.2, Corollary 2.3 and Lemmas 2.5-2.8, printed pp. 1546-1550: quasiregularity of the directional derivatives of solutions, Morrey-Campanato integral estimates, and the freezing/perturbation scheme with the local Riemann-Hilbert problem
Prop. 2.4, printed p. 1548: the local Riemann-Hilbert problem solved with the local Cauchy transform and Beurling transform, whose $L^2$ isometry makes the associated Beltrami operator a contraction
contents.reason: The $L^2$ isometry of the local Beurling transform is the declined singular-integral input; this page's contraction runs instead on the fixed-support Holder space with the bound of the Cauchy-transform lemma.

contents.name: Lemma 3.1, printed pp. 1554-1556: the inverse of a homeomorphic solution solves a nonlinear equation of the same Holder-regular class, and the proof of Theorem 1.1 by the Jacobian identity $J_f(z)J_{f^{-1}}(f(z))=1$
§3 endgame, printed p. 1557: compactness argument giving the lower bound $\inf_{D(0,R_0)}J(z,f)\ge c(H,R_0)>0$ for normalized solutions
contents.reason: The quantitative lower bound for the normalized solution on a fixed disk is not among the claims of this pair; the page proves pointwise positivity of the Jacobian through injectivity of the holomorphic factor instead.

sources.title: John K. Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations (2014)
sources.locator: §2.7.1-§2.7.2, printed pp. 37-43 (PDF pp. 42-48); the named results were read in the source.

contents.name: Theorem 2.26, printed pp. 37-39: the cancelled representation of the second derivatives of the Newtonian potential, $\partial_{ij}u=\int_\Omega\partial_{ij}\Gamma(x-y)(f(y)-f(x))dy-f(x)\int_{\partial\Omega}\partial_i\Gamma(x-y)\nu_j\,dS$
Corollary 2.27, printed p. 39: on a ball containing the support, $\partial_{ij}u=\int_{B_R(x)}\partial_{ij}\Gamma(x-y)(f(y)-f(x))dy-\frac1n\delta_{ij}f(x)$

Theorem 2.28, printed pp. 39-43: the Holder estimate $[\partial_{ij}u]_{0,\alpha}\le C[f]_{0,\alpha}$ for $0<\alpha<1$, by the near/far split, the mean value estimate for the kernel difference and the annular cancellation, with the far integral diverging at $\alpha=1$
§2.8 Singular integral operators, printed pp. 43-46: the Riesz-type operators $T_{ij}$, their homogeneous zero-mean kernels and their $L^2$ boundedness by Plancherel's theorem
contents.reason: Only the fixed-support Holder bound of Theorem 2.28 and the pointwise kernel identities are used on this page; the $L^2$/Plancherel theory of the Riesz-type operators is part of the singular-integral route the binding design declines.
